extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on (1) how to distinguish and interpret assignments vs. licenses in patent instruments (including recordation, assignability, and apportionability), and (2) what constitutes patent infringement (making, using, selling; tests and defenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment vs. license: exclusive right test
rubrics_metrics.description: An instrument is an assignment (and must be recorded) if it vests in the grantee the exclusive right, either for the whole country or for a particular district, of making and using the thing patented and of granting that right to others; if it merely grants a right to make, use, and sell without making that right exclusive, it is a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test to apply is whether the instrument vests the exclusive right and the power to grant that right to others. Example: grant of "right and privilege of making, using, and selling" without exclusivity was held a license (did not require recording). If exclusive right plus right to grant to others appears, treat as assignment (recordation required under statute).

rubrics_metrics.name: District-limited exclusive grants may be assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant conferring the exclusive right to work under the patent for a particular district (limiting quantity or area) will be an assignment if, by its terms, the grantee is authorized to grant to others the right to make and use the patented thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: covenant granting exclusive right to make/use ten machines in a district — if grantee may grant to others rights in those ten, it appears to be an assignment and would transfer an interest in the patent; if the grantee lacks right to grant to others, it remains a license. Construction depends on tenor of whole instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention and contract language can convert exclusive grant into a license
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where exclusive-right language appears, the instrument should be construed according to the parties' intention; provisos for termination, reservation of rent or a percentage (rather than granting an interest in profits), and other clauses showing a personal, revocable arrangement indicate a license rather than an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look at the whole instrument; reservation of payment as rent or percentage and termination clauses are evidence the parties intended a license. The instrument's tenor may control even if absolute exclusive language is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordation requirement hinges on transfer of exclusive grant + power to grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statute, a grant requires recording when it embraces the exclusive right of making and using plus the right to grant to others; a mere exclusive license without that power may not trigger the recording requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., English chancery opinion referenced) treats exclusive licenses as licenses unless the right to grant to others is explicitly added. Practical implication: determine whether recording is required by identifying whether grantee received the power to sublicense/assign the exclusive right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignability of a license depends on its terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a license is assignable depends on the express terms of the license; a mere license to the party without mention of assigns is a personal, non-transmissible privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of the word "assigns" in the granting clause does not necessarily make a personal license assignable if the whole instrument indicates a personal privilege. Parties should draft clearly if assignability is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionability (splitting) of a license requires clear language
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a license can be subdivided (apportioned) so the licensee may grant distinct rights to others depends on the license language; courts require exceedingly clear language to construe a single right as apportionable into fragments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: license to employ six persons held to suggest an entirety not easily split; apportioning a single right among several independent holders raises risks to the patentee (competition, difficulty of oversight). Drafters should state expressly if the right may be divided among separate parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by recitals and admissions in license instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitals or covenants in a license admitting the use of the patented thing or the validity/novelty/sufficiency of the patent may estop the licensee from later denying infringement or invalidity in actions for rent or license dues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a licensee has admitted that what he uses is the patented thing or has admitted patent validity in the deed, he may be precluded (estopped) from asserting contrary defenses in certain suits. However, if the patentee joins issue rather than pleading estoppel, the deed may be evidence but not conclusive; courts examine instrument wording and pleadings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments and restitution when patent turns out void
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who has paid an annuity in consideration of a license and has had the benefit of the license generally cannot recover the money paid if the patent later proves void, on the ground the licensee received the benefit; recovery may be possible if the patent is shown invalid before payment became due and no admissions are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable considerations: licensee who has enjoyed the licensed privilege is usually denied restitution. Parties disputing recovery should examine timing of invalidity, presence of admissions in the deed, and whether the license was relied upon for benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity: licensee's obligations before claiming patentee default
rubrics_metrics.description: In equity, a licensee alleging the patentee's failure to perform under a license contract must have done everything within his power to perform the contract; failure to make stipulated payments when required may subject the licensee to injunction for infringing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: license granted on condition of weekly payment — licensee must pay weekly or may be enjoined. Courts expect licensees to fulfill contractual obligations before asserting patentee breaches as a defense to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory acts constituting infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute grants the patentee the exclusive right of "making, using, and vending to others to be used" the invention; infringement occurs when another person makes, uses, or sells the patented thing without authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute lists acts without fully defining each; courts interpret how "make," "use," and "sell" apply to different subject matters (machines, compositions, processes, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: General test for infringement: availing oneself of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringement occurs when a party avails himself of the patentee's invention without such variation as will constitute a new discovery; equivalently, a copy made after and agreeing with the principle laid down in the specification infringes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, courts compare the defendant's device or method with the patent specification to see whether differences are substantial or merely formal/immaterial. Jury fact-finding often required (see Walton v. Potter guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine patents: making, using, selling each actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: For a machine patent, the patent covers the machine itself and the mode/process of making it; making a patented machine for use or sale is an infringement (even if not ultimately used or sold), using it is an infringement, and selling it is an infringement whether made by the seller or another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leading cases hold making a machine may be infringement if done with intent to use/sell; making purely for philosophical experiment or to test specification may not be infringement. Courts examine intent to determine whether a noncommercial/experimental making is exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent-to-use test for making a machine (experiments vs. infringement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a patented machine is an infringement when it is made for use or for sale; making for mere philosophical experiment or to test the sufficiency of the specification generally will not be treated as infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is whether the party made the machine with intent to deprive the patentee of the lawful rewards (i.e., intent to use or sell). Jurisdictions examine motive and surrounding facts; the legislative amendments suggest each enumerated act (make/use/sell) is a substantive wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive use and liability via agreements/ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may be held responsible for 'using' a patented machine constructively if, for example, he purchases an infringing machine and hires it out, or if contractual arrangements effectively amount to his ownership or hiring of the machine (even if nominally framed as a sale of output).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: contract to purchase all output from a manufacturer — whether this is a 'use' depends on whether the defendant owned/hired the machine or whether the transaction was colorable; fact questions for the jury. Courts will look beyond form to substance: ownership, hiring, and intent to invade the patent right can create liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages principle for acts of making/using/selling
rubrics_metrics.description: When the law gives an action for a particular act (making, using, selling), doing that act imports some damage to the patentee; if no actual damage is proved, nominal damages are recoverable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts hold every violation of the exclusive right imports some damage; plaintiffs need not always show extensive monetary loss to obtain a remedy — statutory treble damages provisions and nominal damages may apply depending on facts and proof.
